summary: pack size is what the Quit smoking and save calculator works out, and it gets there from the packs smoked, the money spent, the cigarettes not smoked and the return on Investment. Think of it as a shortcut for a practical question that turns up in daily life. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Quit smoking and save calculator work?
sections.html:
The Quit smoking and save calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports pack size in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select what to chart); then you type in the packs smoked, the money spent, the cigarettes not smoked and the return on Investment.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as years and months (for periods shorter than 6 years). The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Quit smoking and save calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Pack size=cigarettes smoked ÷ packs smoked
Pack cost=money spent ÷ packs smoked
How long you won't smoke=(1 ÷ 12) × the natural log of ((12 × final savings × return on Investment + money spent) ÷ money spent) ÷ the natural log of (return on Investment + 1)
How long you won't smoke=cigarettes not smoked ÷ cigarettes smoked
Time unit ph=(show result in)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.
  • Shown in years, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Shown in days, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in days
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Time, opening in years
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Time, opening in years
  • %, opening in interest rate per year
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Quit smoking and save calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the packs smoked, the money spent and the cigarettes not smoked — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Quit smoking and save calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns pack size, derived from the packs smoked, the money spent and the cigarettes not smoked. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Quit smoking and save calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the packs smoked, the money spent, the cigarettes not smoked and the return on Investment, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter cigarettes smoked in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Cigarettes smoked opens in days and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Cigarettes not smoked = 1080000. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Quit smoking and save calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
